issues.legal_issue: A delayed application for statutory revision may be treated as an exercise of the authority’s power to revise on its own motion where the governing law permits that power to be exercised at any time and the circumstances disclose a continuing challenge and serious injustice.
material_facts: The borrowers continued to challenge the recovery and sale through successive proceedings rather than allowing the matter to remain dormant.
They had repaid the principal within the period specified in a government-backed interest-waiver scheme, but the sale of their land was later confirmed without that repayment being considered.
The Minister allowed a revision petition after the six-month period for an application by an aggrieved person had passed; no separate application for condonation of delay had been filed.
The governing revision power permitted the State Government to act on its own motion at any time, and the Minister’s exercise of that power was treated by the Supreme Court as suo motu.
issues.conclusion: The revision was not barred by limitation. In the absence of an application for condonation, the Minister’s exercise of power was to be treated as suo motu, and the High Court erred in setting it aside on a technical limitation ground.
issues.legal_principle: Section 108 of the Karnataka Cooperative Societies Act, 1959 permits a person aggrieved to apply for revision within six months, but also permits the State Government to revise suo motu at any time. Section 29(2) of the Limitation Act, 1963 makes the power to condone delay available in the context of a special law. Where the statute leaves the period for suo motu revision open, the power must ordinarily be exercised within a reasonable time (State of Gujarat v. Patil Raghav Natha; Santoshkumar Shivgonda Patil v. Balasaheb Tukaram Shevale). The Court distinguished V.N. Shrikhande v. Anita Sena Fernandes, which concerned an express limitation bar under the Consumer Protection Act. It applied the preference for substantial justice over technical grounds reflected in Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji, State of Haryana v. Chandra Mani, and Dhiraj Singh v. State of Haryana.

rule.if: special_statutory_revision and authority_may_act_on_own_motion_without_fixed_deadline and continuing_challenges and serious_injustice_from_technical_bar

predicates.special_statutory_revision: The proceeding seeks revision under a statutory scheme that provides a revisional power to a public authority.
predicates.authority_may_act_on_own_motion_without_: The governing law permits the authority to initiate revision on its own motion without setting a fixed time limit for doing so.
predicates.continuing_challenges: The affected person has pursued successive challenges rather than leaving the underlying matter dormant.
predicates.serious_injustice_from_technical_bar: Rejecting the revision on a technical time bar would leave a serious alleged injustice unexamined.

issues.definition: When a statutory revision authority can act on its own motion without a fixed deadline, continuing challenges and serious injustice from a technical bar may permit a late revision to be upheld as suo motu.

issues.legal_issue: An auction purchaser does not qualify for protection as a bona fide purchaser where a sale requiring confirmation is confirmed only after the debt has been repaid and the mortgagor was not given the required opportunity to object to the sale.
material_facts: The recovery award directing sale of the mortgaged land was made ex parte, without the borrowers having an opportunity to present their defence and objections.
The auction took place before the borrowers repaid the principal, but the sale was confirmed only after that repayment had been made under the interest-waiver scheme.
The purchaser acquired the land through a sale requiring confirmation by the relevant authority.
The statutory sale procedure required notice to the mortgagor and an opportunity to object, and the sale proclamation procedure required notice and specified information about the property and sale.
issues.conclusion: The auction purchaser was not a bona fide purchaser, and the purchaser’s interest was not entitled to protection.
issues.legal_principle: Section 89(2) of the Karnataka Cooperative Societies Act, 1959 requires prior authorization after hearing the mortgagor’s objections and written notice to specified interested persons before the power of sale is exercised. Rule 38(2)(d) of the Karnataka Cooperative Societies Rules, 1960 requires publication of a sale proclamation and notice to the applicant and defaulter. Where an auction is subject to confirmation, no rights accrue to the purchaser until confirmation (Velji Khimji and Co. v. Official Liquidator of Hindustan Nitro Product (Gujarat) Limited). The Court distinguished the protection of bona fide auction purchasers recognized in Janatha Textiles v. Tax Recovery Officer because the purchaser in this case was not bona fide in light of the circumstances surrounding the sale and confirmation.

rule.if: cooperative_mortgage_auction and sale_requires_confirmation and principal_repaid_before_confirmation and mortgagor_lacked_opportunity_to_object

predicates.cooperative_mortgage_auction: The proceeding concerns an auction to recover a debt secured by mortgaged property.
predicates.sale_requires_confirmation: The auction sale is not complete, and purchaser rights do not accrue, until an authority confirms the sale.
predicates.principal_repaid_before_confirmation: The borrower repaid the principal debt before the authority confirmed the auction sale.
predicates.mortgagor_lacked_opportunity_to_object: The mortgagor was not given the required opportunity to receive notice and present objections before the sale was carried out.

issues.definition: In a mortgage-recovery auction requiring confirmation, repayment before confirmation together with the mortgagor’s lack of an opportunity to object means that the purchaser is not bona fide and the purchaser’s sale rights are not protected.

issues.legal_issue: Confirmation of a mortgage sale is illegal where the borrower has repaid the principal within the period covered by a government-backed interest-waiver scheme and the authority confirms the sale without considering that repayment.
material_facts: The borrowers had defaulted on a loan secured by their agricultural land and the land was auctioned to recover the debt.
A government-backed scheme provided for waiver of interest where eligible borrowers repaid the principal within the specified period.
The borrowers repaid the entire principal within that period, and the repayment was not contested.
The sale was confirmed afterward without consideration of the repayment or the resulting interest waiver.
The borrowers were small farmers and the land was their source of livelihood.
issues.conclusion: The sale and its confirmation were contrary to the government-backed scheme and law, caused a gross miscarriage of justice, and were illegal. The order setting aside the Minister’s decision was therefore reversed, and possession of the land was directed to be returned to the borrowers.
issues.legal_principle: The government-backed interest-waiver scheme, issued pursuant to executive power under Article 162 of the Constitution, required the State to bear the interest where an eligible borrower repaid the principal within the specified period. Section 108 of the Karnataka Cooperative Societies Act, 1959 empowers the State Government to correct an order contrary to law that has resulted in a miscarriage of justice. Article 21 protects livelihood as an integral part of the right to life (Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation).

predicates.mortgage_recovery_sale: The proceeding concerns a sale of mortgaged property to recover a borrower’s debt.
predicates.borrower_repaid_principal_within_waiver_: The borrower repaid the principal within the period specified by a government-backed scheme that provides for interest relief.
predicates.sale_confirmed_without_considering_repay: The authority confirmed the sale without considering the borrower’s qualifying repayment.
predicates.land_is_source_of_livelihood: The property sold is the borrower’s source of livelihood.

issues.definition: When a borrower repays principal within a period qualifying for interest relief and the sale is confirmed without considering that repayment, confirmation is illegal, particularly where the property is the borrower’s livelihood.
